title: Dynamics
tagline: Kinematics and kinetics of particles and rigid bodies: Newton's second law, work and energy, impulse and momentum, impact and motion in three dimensions
summary: Dynamics explains how forces produce motion. The course treats the kinematics of particles in rectangular, normal–tangential and polar coordinates, Newton's second law, work and energy, impulse, momentum and impact, and then the planar kinematics and kinetics of rigid bodies, ending with rotating frames, Euler's equations and gyroscopic motion in three dimensions.
overview: Statics was the special case. This course is the general one, and its single proposition is Newton's second law applied to whatever you choose to isolate - a particle, a system of particles, a rigid body, or a collection of rigid bodies connected by joints. Everything else is bookkeeping: the choice of coordinate system, the choice of method, and the choice of what to call the system.

The course is organised around the two great decompositions of the subject. The first is **kinematics before kinetics**: you cannot write $\sum \mathbf{F} = m \mathbf{a}$ until you know $\mathbf{a}$, and knowing $\mathbf{a}$ is a purely geometric exercise that most students skip and most errors come from. Kinematics of a particle in rectangular, normal-tangential and cylindrical components; the relative-motion framework for translating and rotating axes, with the Coriolis term that appears whenever an observer turns; and then rigid-body kinematics, in which every motion is a translation plus a rotation and every velocity is $\mathbf{v}_B + \boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{r}_{B/A}$. The second decomposition is **the three methods**, and knowing which to use is the actual skill: $\sum \mathbf{F} = m \mathbf{a}$ when forces and accelerations are asked for and time matters; work and energy when the question is speed against position and the forces do no work or do known work; impulse and momentum when the question is speed against time, or when an impact makes the forces unknowable.

Rigid-body kinetics is where the subject becomes mechanical rather than merely mathematical. A rigid body's equations carry an inertia tensor whether you want one or not, and the plane-motion equations $\sum M_G = I_G \alpha$ and $\sum M_P = I_P \alpha +$ a transport term differ in exactly the way that makes the difference between a correct answer and a plausible one. The general plane-kinetics problem - a rolling spool, a slipping ladder, a two-plate mechanism - is solved by drawing one kinetic diagram per body and equating force systems rather than moments, because moments about an arbitrary point are a trap. **The work-energy and impulse-momentum methods then return for rigid bodies, and with them the two terms students least expect: that a rolling body's kinetic energy contains $I_G \omega^2 / 2$ and not $mv^2 / 2$ alone, and that the power of a friction force at a point of zero velocity is zero however large the force.**

The course closes on three-dimensional motion, where the vector equations become matrix equations and two new phenomena appear that have no plane analogue. **Gyroscopic action** is not a mystery but the statement that $\sum \mathbf{M} = d\mathbf{H}/dt$ and that $\mathbf{H}$ need not point along $\boldsymbol{\omega}$; the steady-precession formula, the bearing reactions of a tilted disc and the steering torque of a motorcycle are all one equation. **Dynamic balancing** is the statement that a rotating body can have zero resultant force and a non-zero resultant couple, and that the couple is what shakes a turbine. And **the relative acceleration in rotating frames** - centripetal, tangential and Coriolis together - is the equation that runs weather forecasting, the Foucault pendulum, inertial navigation and the design of every mechanism in the next course. **Dynamics is the last course in this part of the curriculum that adds a new idea; everything after it is the same three equations applied to deformable bodies, to many degrees of freedom, and to machines.**
outcomes: Describe the motion of a particle in rectangular, normal-tangential, cylindrical and path coordinates, convert between them, and compute the velocity and acceleration components for a stated trajectory without differentiating the wrong unit vector
Analyse constrained motion of connected particles and of blocks on cords, pulleys and slots, write the dependent-motion constraints correctly, and extend them to two and three degrees of freedom

Solve the equation of motion for a particle under a force that is a function of time, position or velocity, including rectilinear and curvilinear motion with quadratic drag, and identify which of the three functional forms makes the equation separable

Apply work and energy to particles and to systems of particles, distinguish conservative from non-conservative forces, use the potential function, and compute the efficiency and the power of a machine from the rate of work

Apply linear and angular impulse and momentum to particles and to systems, treat central-force motion and the conservation of angular momentum about a fixed centre, and solve direct and oblique impact with the coefficient of restitution and the correct line of impact

Analyse the plane motion of a rigid body by drawing the free-body and kinetic diagrams together and equating the two force systems, and use the moment equation about an arbitrary point correctly, including the transport term

Combine translation and rotation in the relative-motion description of a rigid body, resolve velocities and accelerations in rotating axes including the Coriolis component, and choose between the translating and rotating frames from what is asked

Solve rigid-body problems by work and energy and by impulse and momentum, computing the general plane-motion kinetic energy and the angular momentum about an arbitrary point, and treat the eccentric blow and the oblique central impact of a rigid body

Write the angular momentum and the equations of motion of an unsymmetrical body in three dimensions, compute the products of inertia and the principal axes, and analyse the steady precession of a gyroscope and the bearing reactions of a rotating unbalanced rotor

Select the appropriate method - force and acceleration, work and energy, or impulse and momentum - from the form of the question, and justify the choice by stating which quantities are conserved, which do no work, and which are impulsive

history.title: The three laws, and the first problem in the Principia
history.detail: Newton's *Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica*, written at Edmond Halley's urging and published at his expense in 1687, states the three laws that are the whole of this course. What is less often noticed is that the *Principia* is a book about astronomy, argued geometrically, and almost never writes an equation in the form an engineer would use. The machinery of components and of the moment equation was added in the eighteenth century — d'Alembert's *Traité de dynamique* of 1743, and Euler, who wrote the second law as differential equations in rectangular components around 1750 and extended it to rigid bodies — and the engineering form of the subject was shaped by the teachers of the Ecole Polytechnique and its successors in the early nineteenth century, among them Poisson, whose *Traité de mécanique* appeared in 1811, Coriolis and Poncelet. **The free-body diagram is not in Newton. It became a standard teaching device only in later engineering textbooks, and it is arguably a harder idea than the second law, because it requires you to see a body as separate from everything it touches.**

history.title: Lagrange, and mechanics without vectors
history.detail: Joseph-Louis Lagrange's *Mechanique analytique* of 1788 - which, as its preface proudly says, contains no figures - recast the whole of mechanics as a set of equations in generalised coordinates, obtained by differentiating one scalar function, in which the workless constraint forces never appear because the coordinates are chosen to satisfy the constraints. In 1834-35 William Rowan Hamilton showed that the same equations follow from the stationarity of an integral of the difference between kinetic and potential energy, and Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi developed the theory further. **Multibody dynamics codes, robot manipulator equations and vibration textbooks are largely Lagrangian, because the vector approach must carry the reaction force at every joint as an extra unknown, while the Lagrangian gives one equation per degree of freedom; the reason this course is nevertheless Newtonian is that the vector approach tells you what the forces are, the Lagrangian tells you what the motion is, and a designer needs both.**

history.title: Coriolis, and the acceleration of a turning observer
history.detail: Gaspard-Gustave Coriolis, who had already written on the work done by machines in 1829, published in 1835 a memoir on the equations of relative motion of systems of bodies, in which he showed that in a rotating frame Newton's law needs, besides the centrifugal term, an extra term proportional to the velocity relative to the frame. The same term had appeared earlier, for instance in Laplace's tidal equations of 1778, but Coriolis gave the general treatment, and his name became attached to the deflection of winds and currents on the rotating Earth in the early twentieth century. **The reason the term is taught twice, once here and once in every mechanism course, is that it can be seen in two ways: as a kinematic consequence of differentiating vectors in a rotating frame, and as the dynamical effect of angular momentum on a body moving towards or away from the axis. Understanding that these are the same statement is the point of the lesson, and it is not obvious.**

history.title: The Foucault pendulum, and dynamics you can stand in
history.detail: Leon Foucault, a thirty-one-year-old physicist without an academic post, showed a pendulum to scientists in the Meridian Room of the Paris Observatory, with Francois Arago's support, in February 1851, and the plane of swing turned at the rate predicted for the Earth's rotation at the latitude of Paris. A public version with a 67-metre wire and a 28-kilogram bob followed in the Pantheon in March 1851, and copies were soon set up in many cities. The next year Foucault built the instrument he named the **gyroscope**, a spinning rotor in gimbals whose axis keeps its direction in space. **The pendulum is the clearest demonstration in physics that the Earth is a rotating reference frame and not an inertial one, and it is the reason the equations of this course carry a term that nobody can switch off. Weather maps, ocean currents and inertial navigation systems all carry the same term.**

history.title: The inertia tensor, and why a body does not spin the way you throw it
history.detail: The idea that angular momentum need not point along the angular velocity is due to the mathematicians of the eighteenth century - Euler's equations for a rigid body date from the 1750s and 1760s, and Poinsot gave them their geometric picture in 1834 - but its engineering consequences were worked out only when rotating machinery became fast. Rankine's analysis of a whirling shaft in 1869 suggested that a shaft could not run stably above its critical speed; Dunkerley measured whirling speeds in 1894; de Laval's steam turbines of the 1880s nevertheless ran above it, Föppl explained why in 1895, and in 1919 Henry Jeffcott published the simple rotor model that still underlies the analysis of critical speeds and unbalance response. **A rigid body has three principal axes, and rotation about only two of them is stable: throw a remote control or a book and watch it flip. That the intermediate axis is unstable is a short consequence of Euler's equations and one of the most beautiful results in elementary dynamics.**

history.title: The space flight problem, and dynamics without a ground
history.detail: For most of its history engineering dynamics dealt with vehicles and machines on the ground, where the Earth could be treated as flat and, for most purposes, inertial. From the launch of Sputnik in 1957 the same three laws had to be applied to vehicles whose propellant is most of their mass, whose trajectories are conic sections and whose attitude is controlled by small torques. The result was not new physics but a re-examination of familiar assumptions: variable-mass systems, gravity-gradient torque and the attitude dynamics of bodies with flexible or liquid-filled parts. Explorer 1, launched in January 1958 spinning about its axis of least inertia, went into a tumble within hours, and Ronald Bracewell and Owen Garriott explained the cause the same year: energy dissipation in its flexible antennas, which drives a body towards rotation about its axis of maximum inertia. **This course ends where that story began, because the three-dimensional dynamics of a body with products of inertia and an applied couple is the same mathematics as the pointing of a spacecraft.**
